paper.title: Cost-effectiveness of pramipexole augmentation for acute phase and maintenance therapy of treatment-resistant depression compared to placebo augmentation: economic evaluation of the PAX-D randomised controlled trial.

source.title: Cost-effectiveness of pramipexole augmentation for acute phase and maintenance therapy of treatment-resistant depression compared to placebo augmentation: economic evaluation of the PAX-D randomised controlled trial.

study.design: Within-trial economic evaluation nested in randomized double-blind PAX-D trial
study.eligibility: Adults at least 18 years, DSM-5 major depression, QIDS-SR16 greater than 10, ongoing antidepressant, lack of response to at least two adequate antidepressant courses (at least four weeks at minimum recommended dose unless tolerability limited)
study.intervention: Immediate-release oral pramipexole nightly, starting 0.25 mg and titrating every three days to target 2.5 mg over four weeks, reductions allowed
study.comparator: Identical placebo augmentation, ongoing antidepressant and usual care in both arms
study.primaryEconomicMeasure: EQ-5D-5L-based QALYs, UK-specific mapping to EQ-5D-3L, baseline-adjusted AUC with linear interpolation
study.statisticalMethods: Baseline/age/sex/time/arm and interaction fixed effects; site and participant random effects for change scores. Cost/effect uncertainty by nonparametric bootstrap; economic missingness after 12 weeks multiply imputed by chained equations, 25 imputations, predictive mean matching, five donors, separate arms, Rubin pooling. Missing-at-random assumption unverified.

claims.statement: The nested PAX-D economic sample had favorable mean QALY-based ICERs in the main NHS analyses, conditional on UK 2022/2023 costs, horizons and WTP. Societal mean cost savings over 48 weeks had uncertainty spanning zero and are not proven savings or a patient-level benefit probability.

Adjusted EQ-5D utility improvements in the economic sample were reported at 12 and 48 weeks, with point utility changes distinct from integrated QALY gains and observed values distinct from imputed longitudinal data. This is the same parent trial, not independent efficacy replication.

Secondary capability cost-effectiveness varied: at the borrowed 20000 GBP threshold, the 48-week NHS YFC probability was 79% and CWLY 44%. Capability thresholds are not established and these outcomes do not prove symptom remission.

The n56 complete-case analysis had a smaller uncertain QALY difference and 54% probability at the NHS 20000 GBP threshold. Positive net-benefit point estimates had confidence intervals spanning zero, and MAR cannot be verified; main economic conclusions require these qualifications.
